editorial:
The Broadway Melody opened at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in February 1929 as MGM's first all-talking, all-singing musical â€” and became the second film in Academy Awards history to win Best Picture, at the ceremony held in April 1930. Directed by Harry Beaumont, it follows the Mahoney sisters (Bessie Love and Anita Page) navigating Broadway ambition and romantic rivalry alongside hoofer Eddie Kearns (Charles King). The songs â€” 'You Were Meant for Me' and the title number â€” were written by lyricist Arthur Freed and composer Nacio Herb Brown, both then under MGM contract; Freed later produced Singin' in the Rain (1952), which recycled several of these same compositions. MGM's copyright on the film passed to Turner Entertainment when Ted Turner acquired the pre-1986 library in 1986, and then to Time Warner in 1996; Warner Bros. Discovery now holds it as part of what is informally called the Turner library.

For a creator, the 1929 print and its integral soundtrack cleared the public-domain threshold on January 1, 2025, as did the underlying Freed-Brown compositions. The original screenplay is equally free â€” there is no prior literary source whose rights could survive the term expiry. The practical trap is the restoration layer: virtually every high-definition copy of this film in commercial circulation is a Warner Archive restoration master, not a raw PD scan. Warner's copyright on that master is thin but real; it covers the creative choices made in the restoration workflow, not the 1929 footage beneath it. A filmmaker needing a PD-clean copy should seek a print-derived transfer that predates Warner's restoration program, or commission a fresh scan from an archival print held at a public institution such as the Library of Congress or George Eastman Museum.
faq: The Freed-Brown songs from this film appear in other productions too â€” are they public domain everywhere?

The underlying musical compositions ('You Were Meant for Me,' 'The Broadway Melody,' etc.) published in 1929 are public domain in the United States as of January 1, 2025. International status varies by country: many jurisdictions use a life-plus-70 term rather than a fixed publication term, so the compositions remain protected abroad until 70 years after the death of the last surviving author (Nacio Herb Brown died in 1964, Arthur Freed in 1973 â€” meaning life-plus-70 protection in those jurisdictions runs through 2043). Check the law of each territory separately before releasing internationally.
If Warner Bros. put this on a streaming service, does that reset the copyright clock?

No. Streaming or selling a public-domain film on a platform does not restore copyright in the underlying 1929 work. What Warner Bros. owns is its own restoration master â€” a derivative work â€” and only that specific master, not the film itself. You are free to copy, distribute, or adapt the 1929 film from a non-Warner PD source without their permission. You cannot, however, rip the Warner streaming version and redistribute it, because that copy is Warner's restoration master, not the original 1929 film.
